title: Perdiccas
capsule: Perdiccas (c. 360–320 BCE) was a senior Macedonian general who became regent of Alexander the Great's empire upon Alexander's death in Babylon in June 323 BCE, receiving the royal signet ring and nominal authority over the kings Philip III Arrhidaeus and the infant Alexander IV. He attempted to hold the empire together against increasingly hostile Diadochi, rejecting Antipater's daughter in marriage and seeking instead Alexander's sister Cleopatra as a dynastic alliance, which alienated Antipater, Craterus, and Antigonus simultaneously. His invasion of Egypt to suppress Ptolemy's seizure of Alexander's funeral cortege ended in catastrophe at the Nile in 320 BCE, where approximately 2,000 soldiers drowned or were taken by crocodiles, precipitating a mutiny in which his officers Seleucus, Peithon, and Antigenes murdered him in his tent. The formal partition of the empire at Triparadisus followed shortly after.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Perdiccas's political role is well-attested in ancient sources (Diodorus, Arrian, Justin), but his administrative territorial extent as regent is inferential rather than cartographically precise.
